oil.summary: Crude suffered a brutal session, with Brent off 6.15% to $86.88/bbl and WTI down 4.23% to $80.43—extending a month-long rout that has now stripped roughly 25% from both benchmarks. The dominant theme is returning supply overwhelming geopolitical risk: despite tanker strikes in the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian attacks on a Bahraini industrial site, the market shrugged off the headlines. Russian export disruptions from Baltic and Black Sea storms provided only fleeting support. On the geopolitical side, Trump's pressure on Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian refineries, his defence of a Russia diesel deal, and an EU proposal to ban European assistance for repairing Russian refineries are all adding political noise. CME OPEC Watch now prices a 77% probability of a production cut at the May 2026 meeting, suggesting the market expects OPEC to respond. Heating oil's 6.84% drop was the sharpest mover on the complex.
drivers: Returning supply overwhelms Hormuz tanker-strike and Russian export disruption risk, sending the entire complex sharply lower
Geopolitical cross-currents: Trump pushes to halt Ukrainian refinery strikes and defends Russia diesel deal while EU advances sanctions on Russian refinery repair
CME OPEC Watch at 77% probability of a cut signals the market anticipates supply-side intervention before prices stabilise

gas.summary: Henry Hub surged 3.69% on the day to $3.537/MMBtu, extending a remarkable month-long rally of nearly 34%. TTF added 3.32% to €91.39/MWh, up 7.84% on the week. The European bid was supported by the EU's advancing legislation to ban Russian gas imports, reinforcing the structural tightening narrative. Cold-weather demand provided an additional catalyst, with Japan's spot electricity prices hitting their highest since August 2022 on snowfall expectations and rising gas burn. The data-centre power story remains a background constructive theme, with ongoing debate about whether batteries can displace gas turbines at scale. Headline newsflow here is relatively thin but directionally consistent: tighter supply policy, rising seasonal demand, and elevated prices across both Atlantic and Pacific Basin benchmarks.
drivers: EU advancing legislation to ban Russian gas imports tightens the structural supply outlook for European TTF
Cold weather arrival in Japan pushes spot electricity to 2022 highs, increasing LNG/gas burn and global demand competition
Henry Hub +34% over the past month signals broader tightening; seasonal heating demand is amplifying the move

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs slipped 1.22% to $77.44/EUA, now down nearly 8% on the week and roughly 6% on the month—a notable divergence from the rising gas input cost reflected in TTF's 3.32% daily gain to €91.39/MWh. The widening gap between gas and carbon prices may reflect reduced clean-spark spread attractiveness and demand-side uncertainty. Japan's electricity spot prices surging to a 2022 high on cold-weather demand is the standout power headline globally. The Pakistan-Iran energy cooperation development and the Russia-China Power of Siberia 2 discussion add geopolitical texture to the longer-term gas-to-power supply picture, though neither item moves markets near-term. The batteries-vs-gas-turbines debate at data centres remains a medium-term structural overhang for gas power demand. Headline coverage for EU power specifically is thin today.
drivers: EUA carbon prices sliding despite higher TTF gas costs, widening the disconnect between input fuel prices and emissions pricing
Japan spot power prices hit a 2022 high on cold-weather demand, highlighting seasonal tightness in gas-fired generation globally
EU Russian gas import ban legislation and Iran-Pakistan electricity cooperation signal continued structural reshaping of power supply chains
